What does it cost a city to forget a river? Not the money, though the money is staggering. Not the property, though whole neighborhoods now negotiate with the flood line every spring. The real cost is quieter. A river you have forgotten is a river that no longer appears in your maps of childhood, in your directions, in your sense of where the town ends. It becomes a rumor running under the parking lots.

We paved it because paving was progress. We culverted it because culverts were tidy. We built the mall above it because the mall needed flat ground and the river, being underground, could not object. Each decision was defensible in its meeting room. That is how these things go. Nobody votes to forget a river. You vote for drainage, for parking, for a tax base, and the forgetting happens by itself, one agenda item at a time.

Ask the residents of Ward Six what the water table is. They know it the way you know a neighbor's habits: by sound, by season, by the stain line in the basement. The city will remember the river eventually. Rivers collect their debts whether or not you kept the receipts.
